# Tuning-run findings: U1/U2 selection comparison (I2-A10, first pass of I2-A04)

**Run:** `experiments/results/u1u2-tuning/`, 30,606 runs, protocol v1 tuning configuration (`experiments/configs/u1u2-tuning.json`, SHA-256 `4d1efaa2…`), generated at commit `272cdfe` with no tracked changes. Default assumed parameters, budget 8, seeds 1000–1299. Figures and captions: `experiments/results/u1u2-tuning/figures/`. Every number below is in `metrics.csv` with its numerator, denominator and 95% interval.

**Read this first.** These are synthetic students generated by stated rules, on a candidate bank awaiting expert acceptance, under assumed parameters. They show how the selection methods and stopping rules behave; they are not accuracy on real students. This is the **tuning** split: it may be used to choose what to investigate. The protocol's comparison claims are made only on the held-out split, which waits for an accepted content version.

## 1. Adaptive versus fixed versus random selection (misconception holders)

Correct coverage = correct label ÷ holder runs (U1 1,200 runs per bar, U2 1,500).

| Unit, apply rate | Adaptive | Fixed order | Random item | Mean questions (A / F / R) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| U1, 0.5 | 57.3% | 57.8% | 52.7% | 3.99 / 4.28 / 4.63 |
| U1, 0.7 | 82.3% | 81.4% | 81.6% | 3.51 / 3.77 / 3.95 |
| U1, 0.9 | 96.9% | 97.1% | 95.3% | 2.90 / 3.11 / 3.20 |
| U2, 0.5 | 53.2% | 40.4% | 43.1% | 3.62 / 6.09 / 4.81 |
| U2, 0.7 | 76.4% | 54.9% | 71.7% | 3.19 / 5.15 / 4.47 |
| U2, 0.9 | 93.1% | 59.8% | 90.9% | 2.71 / 4.57 / 3.90 |

- **U1:** adaptive and fixed reach the same correct coverage (intervals overlap; e.g. 82.3% [80.1, 84.4] vs 81.4% [79.1, 83.5] at 0.7) but adaptive asks fewer questions (3.51 vs 3.77 at 0.7). Random selection gives more wrong labels (wrong-diagnosis rate 2.0% vs 0.3% at 0.7) and asks the most questions.
- **U2:** adaptive is clearly ahead of the fixed order (76.4% vs 54.9% at 0.7) with far fewer questions (3.19 vs 5.15). The fixed order refuses 40–60% of holders and **299 of 300 no-misconception students** (all by budget).

**Why the fixed order fails in U2.** Ranked once at the prior, its first eight items (T2-005 … T2-016) all link the same three misconceptions (MATH-658, MATH-2039, MATH-1715). None triggers MATH-61 or MATH-1965, which predict the correct answer exactly like NONE. A student answering all eight correctly ends with NONE 0.472, MATH-61 0.264, MATH-1965 0.264, and the budget is spent (R5). The adaptive method re-ranks after every answer and moves to items that separate the remaining candidates. This is the clearest evidence in the run for what adaptivity adds: avoiding a non-adaptive order's blind spots, not raising coverage where a static order is already informative (U1).

## 2. Wrong, missed and refused diagnoses under adaptive selection

| | U1 (0.5 / 0.7 / 0.9) | U2 (0.5 / 0.7 / 0.9) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wrong-diagnosis rate (wrong ÷ labelled) | 0.7% / 0.3% / 0.3% | 8.7% / 4.9% / 2.0% |
| Missed (none detected ÷ holder runs) | 37.4% / 15.8% / 2.6% | 40.5% / 19.3% / 5.0% |
| Refused (÷ holder runs) | 4.8% / 1.7% / 0.2% | 1.2% / 0.4% / 0.0% |

- **U2's wrong labels are almost all one confusion:** 154 of 163 are MATH-2039 holders labelled MATH-1965, the subset structure of KF-07 (every MATH-1965 option is also a MATH-2039 option). This is a content/catalogue issue for Harris and the expert (I2-H05), not something a threshold should hide.
- **Missed diagnoses dominate at low apply rates:** a holder who applies the misconception half the time answers correctly elsewhere, which is evidence for NONE (KF-12). Lowering `min_support_none` would make this worse; raising thresholds trades misses for refusals.
- The fixed order's low wrong-diagnosis rate in U2 (0.2–0.3%) comes from refusing instead of labelling, which is why wrong-diagnosis rate must always be read with coverage and refusals.

## 3. Students without the labelled misconception

| | Adaptive U1 | Adaptive U2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No misconception (slip 0.08): false label | 5 / 300 (1.7%) | 1 / 300 (0.3%) |
| Random answering: given a misconception label | 154 / 300 (51.3%) | 165 / 300 (55.0%) |
| Off-catalogue: given a misconception label | 211 / 300 (70.3%) | 120 / 300 (40.0%) |
| Always-A (deterministic) | labelled | labelled |

The adverse cases of I2-A01 persist under every method: about half of random answerers and 40–70% of off-catalogue answerers receive a misconception label. Random item selection lowers always-A labelling only slightly (82–84% of runs). These labels are adverse-response labels: there is no misconception behind them.

## 4. What to investigate next (I2-A04, on this tuning split only)

1. `min_support = 3` (D-3) and θ = 0.90: measure the drop in adverse labelling against the added misses, refusals and questions, per unit and apply rate.
2. MATH-2039 → MATH-1965: rerun with Harris's proposed catalogue/content change for the subset pair as a candidate unit table (not by editing `items.csv`), once proposed.
3. Link grades: rerun when Harris supplies reviewed `S`/`T` grades (I2-H04).
4. Off-catalogue labelling in U1 (70%): inspect which unlinked or weakly linked options lead to labels, for the content review.

No default changes on the basis of this run. Any candidate that looks better here must be confirmed on the held-out split, on the accepted content version, before it is proposed.
